lesson_title: How Rescuers Open a Crushed Car
hook_text: A door bent shut by a crash. No hammer, no saw, no flame allowed. So how do rescuers get in?
clip_script: A car has rolled on the N1. The doors are crushed shut and someone is trapped inside. Rescuers cannot pull the door open, because bent steel beats human arms every time. A hammer would hurt the passenger. A saw is slow and shakes the car. A flame near leaking petrol is out of the question. So they bring out the Jaws of Life. Closed tips go into the door crack. The operator presses a thumb control and the arms open slowly with a force like the weight of ten cars. Where does that force come from? Oil pumped into a cylinder presses on a wide piston. Liquid cannot be squashed, so a small pump becomes a giant push. Then the arms, which are levers, multiply it again. Hydraulics plus levers. That is the problem and the principle behind the whole term, and the model you are going to build.
visual_style: Whiteboard sketch of a rolled car with a jammed door; a beak-shaped spreader slides into the gap and opens, with arrows labelled pump, oil, piston, lever.
mood: Urgent and then reassuring: the problem looks impossible until the principle is revealed.
pacing: Fast setup, three quick rejected tools, slow dramatic reveal of the spreader opening.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write the problem statement for the N1 crash yourself.
